5. On considering the ground for delay as stated above, we find that the file moved from one officer to the other officer within usual and normal gap of time and as such it cannot be said that there had been gross negligence on the part of the Government in filing the appeal. This Bench in a decision reported in (1994) 14 BLD 198 has held that the expression "sufficient cause" contained in section 5 of the Limitation Act" implies presence of adequate reason. It is the circumstances beyond the control of the party including negligence to the extent of which it can be regarded as human, but excluding gross negligence". 

 6. In that decision it has been further observed: "There is no doubt about the legal position that the law of limitation operates equally for or against the private party and also on the Government. But it is a fact which must be accepted that a private litigant is normally presumed to be aware of all the factors and aspect of his case and he has only to make up his own mind as to pursue further of his litigation, whereas in the case of Government, a longer time is required for enquiry and consideration vis-a-vis public interest by not only one agency, but several ones before taking final decision and thereafter, acting thereon. Thus, period of time which may be sufficient for a private litigant may not be so for Government. The court is to consider in the case for the latter whether a Government Department in question has acted bonafide or has been grossly negligent in prosecuting its case and if the Court comes to the conclusion that there has been no gross negligence the Court should condone the delay disregarding the length of the delay".
